lessons.title: Meet your guitar
lessons.summary: Find your way around the instrument.
lessons.see: Rest the guitar securely and let your shoulders relax. The thinnest string is 1; the thickest is 6. A fret number names the space just before that metal fret. Touch a string on the diagram to explore it.
lessons.detail: Your fretting fingers are index 1, middle 2, ring 3, and little finger 4. Press just behind the fret, not on its wire, using only enough pressure for a clear note. Pick one string gently. Pause if anything hurts.
lessons.practice: Play each reference tone and match your open string by ear, or use your own tuner. These are reference pitches, not automatic tuning measurements. Spend a minute finding strings 1 and 6 without rushing.
lessons.recap: You can name the strings, find a fret, and identify your fretting fingers.

lessons.title: Six open strings
lessons.see: An open string rings without a fretting finger. Read the board from string 6 to string 1: E, A, D, G, B, E. The two E strings share a letter but sound two octaves apart.
lessons.detail: The hollow circle means open: no fretting finger. The staff uses guitar treble notation, written one octave above what you hear. A sounding high-string E4 is written as E5; the tab and fretboard still mean the open first string.
lessons.practice: Play each open string slowly. Say its name before picking. Then try returning from high E to low E. Repeat twice, leaving time to move your picking hand.
lessons.recap: You have connected six open-string sounds to names and locations.

lessons.title: Your first three notes
lessons.summary: E, F, and G on string 1.
lessons.see: Keep your hand near the nut. Play E open, F with finger 1 at fret 1, and G with finger 3 at fret 3. This is first position: your fingers work near frets 1–4.
lessons.detail: The number inside a lit marker is your finger, not the fret number. Read the fret along the bottom edge. Keep unused fingers relaxed and close to the string.
lessons.practice: Step through E, F, G, F. Say each name and place your finger before picking. Repeat the phrase three times, then try finding F with the labels as your guide.
lessons.recap: You can play E–F–G without moving your hand out of first position.

lessons.title: A second string
lessons.summary: B, C, and D; then cross to string 1.
lessons.see: String 2 gives you B open, C at fret 1 with finger 1, and D at fret 3 with finger 3. Check the string number before placing the finger.
lessons.detail: When crossing strings, move the picking hand only as far as needed. The next-note marker shows where to prepare. Listen for one clear note at a time.
lessons.practice: Play B–C–D, then cross to the open E on string 1. Try the return journey slowly. If a string buzzes, reset your fingertip just behind the fret.
lessons.recap: You can connect two strings into a short musical phrase.

lessons.title: Into the middle
lessons.summary: G–A and D–E–F on strings 3 and 4.
lessons.see: On string 3, play G open and A at fret 2 with finger 2. On string 4, play D open, E at fret 2 with finger 2, and F at fret 3 with finger 3.
lessons.detail: Some note letters appear in several octaves. Use the staff height and string number together. These middle-string notes sound lower than the notes from your first two strings.
lessons.practice: Explore each string separately, then join the phrase. Keep the wrist comfortable and let your elbow move naturally as you reach another string.
lessons.recap: You have extended your first-position map to the middle strings.

lessons.title: The bass strings
lessons.see: String 5: A open, B at fret 2 with finger 2, C at fret 3 with finger 3. String 6: E open, F at fret 1 with finger 1, G at fret 3 with finger 3.
lessons.detail: Bass notes use ledger lines below the staff. Follow one line or space at a time rather than guessing from the distance. The board labels always show the sounding octave.
lessons.practice: Play the bass phrase at an easy tempo. Compare the low open E with the high open E from lesson 2. Keep the string order clear as you move between strings 6 and 5.
lessons.recap: You can locate natural notes across all six strings in first position.

lessons.title: Keep the pulse
lessons.see: In 4/4, count 1–2–3–4 evenly. A quarter note lasts one beat, a half note two beats, and two eighth notes divide one beat: say “1 and”. A rest is counted silence.
lessons.detail: The cursor keeps moving during a rest while the sounding marker disappears. Stop the string gently for a rest. BPM here counts quarter-note beats.
lessons.practice: Clap the rhythm first. Then play it on open E. Start slowly and count aloud. Try three loops, keeping the rests as steady as the notes.
lessons.recap: You can keep counting through long notes, short notes, and rests.

lessons.title: Your first melody
lessons.see: Use the notes you already know to play this original melody. Read a few notes ahead and prepare the next finger while the current note sounds.
lessons.detail: Practice the two bars separately, then join them. Long notes are a chance to breathe and prepare, not a reason to lose the beat.
lessons.practice: Choose a tempo where you can stay relaxed. Play one phrase, pause to reset, and play it again. Aim for a steady pulse rather than speed.
lessons.recap: You can combine note reading, string changes, and rhythm into a melody.

lessons.title: E minor
lessons.see: Place finger 2 on string 5 at fret 2 and finger 3 on string 4 at fret 2. Leave strings 6, 3, 2, and 1 open. Together these notes form E minor, written Em.
lessons.detail: A chord sounds several notes together. The board shows the whole shape. First check each string separately so you can hear whether every intended note rings.
lessons.practice: Choose String check and pick from string 6 to 1. Adjust any muffled note, then choose Chord to hear all six together. Strum gently downward and let it ring for four beats.
lessons.recap: You can build Em and check each of its six strings.

lessons.title: A minor
lessons.summary: Build Am and make a slow chord change.
lessons.see: For Am, place finger 1 on string 2 fret 1, finger 2 on string 4 fret 2, and finger 3 on string 3 fret 2. Play strings 5 through 1; leave string 6 out.
lessons.detail: An X means do not play that string. Check the five intended strings individually. Move slowly between Em and Am, letting the shape settle before the next strum.
lessons.practice: Practice the Am string check, then the Changes phrase. Strum on beat 1 and use the remaining beats to prepare. Pause between changes whenever you need to.
lessons.recap: You can form Am and move between two open chord shapes.

lessons.title: D major
lessons.summary: A smaller chord with a sharp.
lessons.see: Place finger 1 on string 3 fret 2, finger 3 on string 2 fret 3, and finger 2 on string 1 fret 2. Play from open string 4 down toward string 1. Omit strings 5 and 6.
lessons.detail: String 1 fret 2 is F-sharp: one fret above F. The sharp sign raises a note by one semitone. This F-sharp helps give D major its sound.
lessons.practice: Check the four strings separately. Keep fingertips curved enough for adjacent strings to ring, without forcing your hand. Then try one gentle four-string strum every four beats.
lessons.recap: You can read a sharp and form the open D-major shape.

lessons.title: Put it together
lessons.summary: Finish with melody and chord changes.
lessons.see: First play the melody using single notes. Then choose Chord changes for a separate Em–Am–D exercise. These are two activities: you do not need to play melody and chords at once.
lessons.detail: Review the notes or chord shapes whenever you need to. Progress means taking part and noticing what to practice next, not passing a speed test.
lessons.practice: Spend a minute on the melody and a minute changing chords slowly. Finish by choosing one earlier lesson to revisit. A few relaxed minutes repeated regularly are enough for a useful practice session.
lessons.recap: You have explored open strings, first-position notes, rhythm, a melody, and three chord shapes. Keep revisiting them at your own pace.
